As a clinician working with long-COVID and other complex patients, I think this video oversimplifies the study and risks misleading people. This trial does NOT “debunk” NR. What it actually shows is: • NR clearly increases NAD⁺ (so the biological target is real) • primary outcomes were negative for the whole mixed cohort • exploratory data suggested possible benefit over ~10 weeks • and critically — the study did NOT stratify patients by biology (e.g., low vs normal NAD⁺), despite long-COVID being extremely heterogeneous In clinical science, a negative average result in a heterogeneous group does NOT equal “this doesn’t work.” It usually means there are responders and non-responders, and the trial wasn’t designed to identify them. We already learned this in migraine, depression, autoimmune disease, asthma… progress came from subgrouping, not from declaring blanket conclusions. The responsible takeaway is: NR safely raises NAD⁺; it didn’t outperform placebo across everyone; we urgently need subgroup-focused studies (e.g., patients with demonstrably low NAD⁺ or mitochondrial dysfunction) — not all-or-nothing claims. Science deserves nuance. Patients deserve it even more.

Nicotinamide (NAM) and nicotinic acid (NA) enter NAD+ synthesis through completely different routes. NAM goes through the salvage pathway via NAMPT, NA goes through the Preiss Handler pathway via NAPRT. These aren't interchangeable. The critical issue: NAMPT is the rate limiting enzyme in the entire NAD+ biosynthetic network. It has a low Vmax and is circadian regulated. If you take cheap B3 (nicotinamide), every molecule must pass through this bottleneck. NMN bypasses NAMPT entirely, that's the whole point of supplementing it. It gets worse. At high doses, free nicotinamide actually inhibits sirtuins through product feedback inhibition. NAM is what gets released when sirtuins consume NAD+, so flooding the system with it suppresses the very enzymes you're trying to fuel. NMN doesn't have this problem because it converts directly to NAD+ via NMNAT without existing as free nicotinamide until the NAD+ is actually used. And if you go the niacin (nicotinic acid) route instead, you hit flushing, hepatotoxicity risk, and insulin resistance at the doses needed to meaningfully elevate NAD+. For the NMN vs NR debate: NR is one enzymatic step behind NMN in the salvage pathway. NR must be phosphorylated by NRK1/NRK2 to become NMN, which then gets converted to NAD+ by NMNAT. So NR requires two enzymatic steps to reach NAD+ while NMN requires one. NRK expression is tissue variable, meaning NR conversion efficiency depends on which tissue you're looking at. More importantly, NR has a worse degradation profile. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase and other nucleosidases in the gut can cleave NR's glycosidic bond, liberating free nicotinamide plus ribose. That free nicotinamide now hits the NAMPT bottleneck we just discussed. NMN's degradation pathway is more graceful, the worst that happens is CD73 strips its phosphate group, converting it to NR. So NMN's degradation product is NR, while NR's degradation product is free nicotinamide. NMN fails up, NR fails down. At 1000mg oral NMN, you also saturate CD73 at the brush border, meaning excess NMN beyond what CD73 can process is available for intact absorption. The higher you dose, the more you overwhelm the dephosphorylation bottleneck and the more intact NMN gets through. Yes, some fraction of oral NMN gets degraded before absorption. But the Yoshino 2021 clinical trial at WashU showed significant NAD+ elevation and metabolic improvement with NMN specifically. That data doesn't exist for high dose niacin as an NAD+ repletion strategy. Saying "it all becomes B3 anyway" is like saying you don't need protein because amino acids get broken down and reassembled just eat nitrogen. The pathway matters, the rate limiters matter, and the clinical data exists for NMN, not niacin.

Dr. Stansfield makes some legitimate points that I take seriously — the gut bacteria conversion finding is real science, the Bergen study's 6-person sample is genuinely too small to draw conclusions from, and the meta-analysis showing no significant improvements in over-60s is data worth acknowledging honestly. I'm not dismissing his research. However his central conclusion that NMN is essentially overpriced niacin contains several significant logical gaps that I think fundamentally undermine his argument when applied to my specific situation. His most critical error in my view is extrapolating from elderly restoration studies to conclude supplementation is worthless for everyone. Every trial he cites was conducted in people over 60 trying to restore severely depleted NAD after decades of decline. That's not me. I started NMN at 18 with healthy NAD levels and the relevant question for my situation is whether continuous maintenance prevents the decline trajectory entirely — a population that has literally never been studied. Concluding prevention doesn't work based on restoration failure in elderly patients is like studying whether physical therapy helps sedentary 70-year-olds regain muscle and concluding exercise doesn't work for anyone. The studies he cites simply didn't study someone like me. His nicotinic acid conversion argument also cuts both ways in ways he doesn't fully address. Even if NMN converts to nicotinic acid via gut bacteria before being rebuilt into NAD, the end product is still elevated cellular NAD fueling sirtuins, PARPs, and mitochondrial function — the destination matters more than the route. His long COVID example actually proves the mechanism works perfectly since NAD tripled exactly as claimed, it simply wasn't the limiting factor in long COVID symptom resolution. Using that as evidence against NMN's core NAD-raising mechanism is a logical non sequitur that I don't find convincing. My personal experience of 6 years taking NMN starting at 18 directly contradicts his conclusion that raising NAD doesn't translate into anything you'd actually notice. More compellingly, I ran my own controlled experiment by stopping NMN for several months and experienced consistent immune decline across multiple isolated periods that reversed predictably each time I restarted. That dose-response consistency is very difficult to explain away as placebo effect and represents more rigorous self-experimentation than most people conduct. You're right that the video (by Dr. Brad Stanfield) leans heavily skeptical and highlights negative or null human trials, while downplaying mechanisms, animal data, and anecdotal/personal reports.Supplement debates often involve financial incentives on all sides (NR/NMN companies vs. general "debunking" creators), publication bias, and the challenge of proving subtle anti-aging effects in short human RCTs. Here's a fair breakdown addressing your points with evidence. NAD Decline and Preclinical Promise NAD+ levels do decline with age in tissues, correlating with mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced sirtuin activity, inflammation, etc. David Sinclair's lab and others showed NMN(and NR in other studies) reversing aspects of this in mice: better insulin sensitivity, energy metabolism, physical activity, eye function, and some "age-related diseases." These aren't useless—mouse models (especially progeroid or high-fat diet ones) often show clear benefits in tissues like muscle, liver, and brain. Limitations: Mice metabolize these differently (higher doses relative to body weight, shorter lifespans). Human translation is harder. Sinclair's work has faced replication/criticism debates, but the core NAD-boosting biology holds up across many labs. Injectable NAD or precursors giving "super energy" aligns with anecdotal reports and some acute metabolic shifts—likely real for some users via mitochondrial or vascular effects, even if not universal. NR vs NMN Blood Levels and Conversion to Niacin The video's core argument: Both largely convert to nicotinic acid (NA/niacin)via gut bacteria (Princeton isotope tracing, Japanese IV bypass study, ex vivo gut data). Elevated NAAD metabolite "fingerprint" supports Preiss-Handler pathway dominance. Thus, expensive NR/NMN ≈ cheap niacin. Counterpoints: Larger head-to-head (Nature Metabolism, n=65): NR and NMN both roughly doubled circulating NAD+ after 14 days, no big difference. Some human trials show NMN raising muscle NAD metabolites or functional markers where niacin alone might not match (e.g., one 250mg NMN trial in older men improved muscle strength/performance). Gut conversion isn't 100% for everyone; individual microbiome, dose, formulation (sublingual, liposomal), and timing matter. Direct cellular uptake pathways exist too (NR kinases, etc.). Niacin causes flushing and has different side-effect/tissue profiles—NR/NMN are often better tolerated at high doses. If it all reduced to plain B3, why do some trials show differential effects? Biology is nuanced; precursors may influence gut microbiota (e.g., short-chain fatty acids) beyond just NAD. Your skepticism about "debunking studies" popping up for popular non-patented supps is valid—funding, outcome selection, and population matter. Human Outcome Trials: Why Mixed/Null Results Don't Disprove Everything Muscle/strength meta (older adults): No significant gains in mass, grip, gait, chair stand. Video cites this heavily. Your point holds: Many trials didn't mandate or track exercise. NAD boosters may amplify training/mitophagy/autophagy rather than work standalone. Sedentary older people might see minimal functional change. Better studies could pair with resistance training or measure mitochondria directly (e.g., respiration, OXPHOS genes). Glucose/lipids: Meta showed little effect. Fair criticism for metabolic claims. Skin rejuvenation: You noticed tighter neck skin/younger face—plausible. Some NMN trials and anecdotal/celebrity reports (common in longevity circles) note improvements in elasticity, wrinkles, or pigmentation via sirtuins, collagen, or inflammation reduction. Human evidence is weaker than for energy/mice, but not zero. Long COVID trial: NR tripled NAD but no major group differences in cognition/fatigue. Small n, high dropout, specific pathology (possibly spike-related inflammation/oxidative stress not fully fixed by NAD alone). Doesn't disprove general aging benefits. Post-hoc within-group improvements in some symptoms noted in reports. Wrong population for broad claims. Exercise-trained older adults can have youthful NAD levels—lifestyle first is always key. But that doesn't mean supplements add nothing on top. Big Pharma/Confounding Factors This is conspiratorial but has kernels of truth: Supplements aren't patentable like drugs, so less incentive for massive long-term outcome trials. Negative studies get amplified if they fit narratives. Fish oil's saga (early benefits, later mixed due to dose/population/oxidation) is a good analogy—EPA/DHA still have solid plaque/heart data in subgroups. Same for vitamin D, etc. NAD research is young; industry-funded positive studies exist alongside independent nulls. Many MDs (longevity-focused) promote it based on mechanisms + anecdotes + safety. B3 (niacin) alone: Doesn't replicate Sinclair mouse "reversal" as dramatically in literature—different pharmacokinetics and tissue delivery. Bottom Line: Not "Useless," But Overhyped for Some Claims Strong: Safely and reliably raises blood NAD+ in humans. Preclinical promise is excellent. Personal energy/skin benefits reported widely (including yours). Weak: Consistent functional outcomes in broad human RCTs (especially sedentary elderly, short-term). Expensive if gut conversion dominates. Not a miracle. Promising angles: Mitochondria function, mitophagy, exercise synergy, specific tissues (skin, brain?), longer trials, biomarkers beyond strength tests. Try tracking objective markers (e.g., VO2 max, inflammation, skin elasticity scans, or even simple energy/activity logs) if continuing. Lifestyle (exercise, sleep, calorie control) remains the best-proven "anti-aging." NAD precursors are low-risk tools that can help for some, especially if you notice benefits—science is incomplete, not settled against them. The video cherry-picks nulls while the full picture (mice + mechanisms + anecdotes + some positive human data) supports cautious optimism.

NR* can use the NRK pathway *directly in cells**, potentially bypassing rate-limiting steps (like NAMPT enzyme, which is often downregulated in aging). Even if much converts to NA later, the initial routing can produce more NAD+ in key tissues. Nicotinamide (NAM)** can inhibit sirtuins at high levels — NR/NMN avoid this issue better. As someone who understands how study design and the pool of subjects chosen can have a major influence on the outcomes, I'd have to say that there is a lot to be desired regarding most of the NMN studies done -- irrespective of whether they were industry sponsored or done via academic centers with no financial interest. First of all, the pool of participants for the studies were all too small (well below a hundred, let alone the gold standard of a thousand), and the endpoints chosen (with the exception of metrics like HbA1C) not the most clinically substantive, if not conclusive. Which matters when considering we still do not know a lot about NMN, especially when trying to ascertain outcomes data from short and simple study designs which seemed to vacillate like moving goal posts... To be sure, NMN is a rather delicate metabolite that can degrade quickly in the body. It has a short window of utility, making it unlike vitamin D which the body can store for use later. The window of opportunity for its use as a nutraceutical regarding its efficacy remains both elusive and varied person to person, which may or may not be dependent on a myriad of other factors depending on what it is you're looking for. That said, what is indisputable however is the fact that many have observed first hand benefits from taking it (including yours truly). Is it all a case of mass placebo effect? I think not... While the hype around NMN as a cure all against aging has died down (no pun intended), whether or not it can benefit our lifestyle regimen as it relates to things like exercise, and whether it can actually mitigate age related degradation of our epigenome, a much larger, and more conclusive longitudinal data set is needed. Due to the relative newness of this active ingredient (now sanctioned by the FDA from being sold as a dietary supplement) the only clinical data we can cite conclusively at this stage is its safety in the near term, something which many may be able to agree on.
